entries.title: Scythian and related steppe traditions
entries.location: Eurasian steppe · Black Sea to Siberia and Central Asia
entries.note: A broad archaeological frame for varied mobile communities, regional cultures and ruling groups. Shared horse-riding and artistic traditions do not imply one united empire or a single ancestry for later peoples. The dates are approximate.

entries.title: Xiongnu confederation
entries.dates: c. 209 BC–93 AD · selected imperial frame
entries.location: Mongolian plateau and neighbouring Inner Asia
entries.note: An empire brought diverse communities into far-reaching political and exchange networks. The conventional 93 AD endpoint concerns the northern imperial formation; southern Xiongnu governments and communities continued. This is not an ethnic extinction date.

entries.title: First Turkic Khaganate · early imperial phase
entries.location: Mongolian plateau and Central Asian steppe
entries.note: Founded under Bumin, this imperial formation soon developed eastern and western centres. Civil conflict and separation unfolded over decades from the late sixth century; c. 603 is a conventional division marker, not an instantaneous split of a uniformly governed territory.

entries.title: Eastern Turkic Khaganate · independent phase
entries.location: Mongolian plateau and adjacent Inner Asia
entries.note: Selected post-division phase of eastern Türk rule, ending with Tang military defeat in 630. Earlier eastern government, subsequent Tang arrangements and later restored Türk rule are separate frames; these dates do not delimit all Turkic communities.

entries.title: Western Turkic Khaganate · independent phase
entries.location: Central Asia · Semirechye and neighbouring territories
entries.note: The western ruling centre connected steppe alliances and oasis societies. Separation from eastern rulers was gradual. 657 marks the defeat of a principal independent ruler by Tang forces; local rulers, contested authority and related confederations continued afterward.

entries.title: Second Turkic Khaganate
entries.note: Restored Türk imperial rule developed after rebellion against Tang dominance. A coalition including Uyghur, Basmil and Karluk forces overthrew the khaganate; final resistance continued beyond conventional 744. These are state phases, not the full history of Turkic-speaking peoples.

entries.title: Uyghur Khaganate · Orkhon empire
entries.location: Orkhon Valley and wider Mongolian plateau
entries.note: An imperial confederation centred on Karabalghasun interacted closely with Tang China. 840 marks the collapse of this steppe empire; Uyghur communities and later oasis kingdoms continued. It is distinct from those later kingdoms and from modern identities and borders.

entries.title: Sogdian cities and merchant networks
entries.dates: c. 4th–8th centuries AD · selected cultural phase
entries.location: Sogdiana · present-day Uzbekistan and Tajikistan; networks across Asia
entries.note: Agriculture, urban centres, merchants and diasporic communities supported wide cultural exchange. This selected flourishing phase groups several cities and local powers rather than one empire. Sogdian history began earlier and transformations continued after these rounded century anchors.

entries.title: Saba / Sheba · South Arabian kingdom
entries.note: A selected broad phase of Sabaean political power linked irrigation agriculture, cities, sanctuaries and incense trade. UNESCO supplies the approximate range used here; other chronologies begin earlier. The wider Marib archaeological landscape remained active beyond this kingdom frame.

entries.title: Himyar · pre-Aksumite ruling phase
entries.note: A southern Arabian kingdom expanded among neighbouring states and adopted royal monotheism in late antiquity. The approximate starting anchor selects a later portion of its early development; 525 marks Aksumite intervention, not the end of South Arabian society.

entries.title: Nabataean kingdom · royal phase
entries.dates: c. 168 BC–106 AD · selected royal frame
entries.location: Petra, Hegra and surrounding northern Arabia / southern Levant
entries.note: Petra Museum dates this royal frame to 168 BC–106 AD. Nabataean communities and Petra existed earlier. Roman annexation in 106 ended the independent kingdom while settlements, language and traditions continued under changing rule.

entries.title: First Saudi state · Diriyah
entries.location: Diriyah and changing territories of the Arabian Peninsula
entries.note: 1727 marks Muhammad bin Saud’s accession and the official Saudi founding convention. 1744 marks Ibn Abd al-Wahhab’s move to Diriyah and their religious-political alliance, often used as a founding date in historical writing. Ottoman-Egyptian forces captured Diriyah in 1818.

entries.title: Second Saudi state · Najd
entries.note: Saudi rule was restored from Riyadh after an interruption following the fall of Diriyah. Civil conflict and changing territorial control marked this state; Rashidi ascendancy ended it in 1891. It was not uninterrupted rule over the boundaries of today’s Saudi Arabia.

entries.title: Saudi expansion and unification
entries.location: Riyadh, Najd, al-Ahsa, Hejaz and neighbouring Arabian territories
entries.note: A formation period from Ibn Saud’s capture of Riyadh to proclamation of Saudi Arabia. Several emirate, sultanate and dual-monarchy arrangements fall within it, including the existing Hejaz–Nejd entry. This groups campaigns and state changes rather than implying a single unchanged state since 1902.

entries.title: Urartu / Kingdom of Van
entries.location: Armenian Highlands · Lake Van, eastern Anatolia and southern Caucasus
entries.note: A powerful kingdom developed around Lake Van and built fortified centres across the highlands. Its origins and collapse are approximate; this follows the History Museum of Armenia’s broad chronology. Shared territory with later Armenia does not establish a simple ethnic or political succession to any modern state.

entries.title: Arsacid Armenia · royal period
entries.location: Armenian Highlands · between Roman and Iranian spheres
entries.note: The conventional period of Arsacid royal rule includes contested authority, outside intervention and partition. The dynasty’s end in 428 in the Persian sector did not end Armenian society, churches or language. Earlier Armenian kingdoms lie outside this selected frame.

entries.title: Bagratid Armenian kingdom
entries.location: Armenian Highlands · later capital at Ani
entries.note: Ashot I’s recognition restored Armenian kingship; sources differ between 884 and 885. Ani became the capital in 961. The end of the principal Bagratid kingdom did not end other Armenian kingdoms or communities, and medieval Armenia should not be read through today’s borders.

entries.title: Cilician Armenia · principality and kingdom
entries.location: Cilicia · northeastern Mediterranean coast, present-day Türkiye
entries.note: An Armenian principality developed in Cilicia, outside the Armenian Highlands; royal coronation followed in 1198/99. Its court linked Mediterranean and Mongol worlds. The Mamluk capture of Sis in 1375 ended the kingdom, while Armenian communities and cultural traditions continued.

entries.title: Kingdom of Georgia · medieval royal frame
entries.location: Southern Caucasus · changing territory around present-day Georgia
entries.note: Bagrat III’s consolidation began a medieval royal formation whose reach changed substantially. Later invasions, subordinate rule, fragmentation and reunification prevent treating the span as continuous centralized control. By 1490 several kingdoms and principalities were recognised; Georgian history continued in them.
